verifiedBy: LLM review, authorised by repo owner

allowedPatterns: Ich denke + , dass + <clause with the verb LAST>

rules.text: THE TRUE LAW BEHIND THE SLOGAN, stated at last. weil sends the finite verb to the END of its clause — Ich möchte Tee, weil ich müde bin — and denn does not: Ich möchte Tee, denn ich bin müde. Same meaning, same two facts, one word apart, and the word order flips. The slogan is "German puts the verb at the end", which M3 already had to correct once. The law: a SUBORDINATING conjunction (weil, dass, wenn) sends the finite verb last; a COORDINATING one (denn, und, aber, oder) leaves the clause exactly as it would have been and the verb stays second.

deshalb IS THE CONSEQUENCE WORD AND IT IS FRONTED, so it inverts: Ich bin müde. Deshalb möchte ich Tee. It occupies the first position of its own clause — unlike denn, which does not — so the verb comes straight after it and the subject follows the verb. That is M4's verb-second law for the third time, and here it is the thing that tells deshalb apart from denn.

THE haben STATES: German says you HAVE hunger, thirst and fear where English says you ARE hungry, thirsty and afraid. Ich habe Hunger, Ich habe Durst, Ich habe Angst — haben plus a BARE noun with no article at all. The classic slip is *Ich bin Hunger, which does not mean "I am hungry": Hunger is a noun, so it says "I am hunger", which is not a sentence anybody can act on.

THE DATIVE EXPERIENCER RETURNS, and M2 is what paid for it. Temperature is Mir ist kalt — literally "to-me is cold" — with the person in the dative and no subject in the sentence at all. The slogan is "Germans say ich bin kalt for I am cold". The law: Ich bin kalt is a perfectly grammatical German sentence and it means the speaker is cold-HEARTED, so this is not a near miss to be forgiven but a different statement. It is the same construction as M2's Wie geht es Ihnen? and Mir geht es gut, meeting the learner a second time.

dass IS NEVER OPTIONAL. English drops "that" freely — "I think it is good" — and German cannot: Ich denke, dass das Buch gut ist. dass is doing two jobs at once, holding the clause onto the sentence AND sending the finite verb to the end, so leaving it out breaks both. The comma in front of it is obligatory in writing, which English's comma rules are not.

das AND dass ARE TWO DIFFERENT SPELLINGS FOR TWO DIFFERENT WORDS, and the collision is in the anglophone's EAR, not in the writing. dass with two s is the conjunction that opens a clause; das with one is the neuter article and the pointing "that". Ich denke, dass das Buch gut ist has both, one after the other. The word index gives them separate entries because German gives them separate spellings — nothing merges them, and nothing excuses writing one for the other.

warum ASKS FOR THE REASON AND KEEPS THE VERB SECOND: Warum möchten Sie Tee? The answer can be a full sentence, or it can be a bare weil-clause on its own — Weil ich müde bin — with the verb still at the end. That fragment is ordinary spoken German, not a shortcut.

THE COMMA BEFORE A JOINED CLAUSE IS OBLIGATORY in German writing, before weil, denn and dass alike. English puts a comma there when it feels like it; German puts one there because the clause boundary is real. It is a small rule and it never has an exception at this level.

sentences.display: Ich möchte Tee, weil ich müde bin
sentences.cue: I'd like tea because I'm tired
sentences.literal: I would-like tea, because I tired am

words.note: because — SUBORDINATING, so it sends its clause's finite verb to the very end: weil ich müde bin, not *weil ich bin müde. Only the verb moves, all the way. English's “because” moves nothing.

sentences.trap: Only the FINITE verb goes to the end. In a longer weil-clause everything else stays where it was and the one verb carrying the person jumps over all of it — so the clause reads normally until the last word, and then the verb arrives.
sentences.sound: vile — the German w is a v and the ei is "eye", so weil sounds like English "vile". müde is MÜ-duh, with the ü of pursed lips and a voiced final -e.

mistake.display: Ich möchte Tee, weil ich bin müde
mistake.why: weil is subordinating, so the finite verb goes to the end of its clause: weil ich müde bin. Leaving bin in second position is the English order, and it is the single commonest German mistake an English speaker makes.

sentences.usage: Giving a reason for what you have just asked for.
sentences.mnemonic: weil pushes the verb to the wall.

sentences.display: Ich möchte Tee, denn ich bin müde
sentences.cue: I'd like tea, because I'm tired

words.note: because — weil's meaning, the opposite grammar. denn is COORDINATING: it joins two full clauses and changes nothing inside them, so the verb stays second. The word order is the lesson.

sentences.trap: This sentence and the one before it mean the same thing and are built the opposite way round. The conjunction is the ONLY thing that decides: weil moves the verb, denn leaves it alone. Nothing in the meaning tells you which is which.
sentences.sound: den, one short syllable, with a plain d. It sounds like English "den" and shares nothing with it.

variations.display: Ich möchte Kaffee, denn ich bin müde
variations.cue: I'd like coffee, because I'm tired
variations.changed: a different drink; the denn clause keeps its verb second

variations.display: Ich gehe nach Hause, denn ich bin müde
variations.cue: I'm going home, because I'm tired
variations.changed: a different main clause, with the same reason attached

variations.display: Ich möchte Tee, denn ich habe Durst
variations.cue: I'd like tea, because I'm thirsty
variations.changed: a haben state as the reason — habe is still the second element

mistake.display: Ich möchte Tee, denn ich müde bin
mistake.why: denn is coordinating and does not touch the clause after it, so the verb stays second: denn ich bin müde. Sending it to the end is the weil rule applied to the wrong word.

sentences.usage: The same reason, said the way it reads in a notice or a careful sentence.
sentences.mnemonic: denn leaves everything where it found it.
sentences.literal: I would-like tea, for I am tired

words.note: therefore, that's why — the consequence word, pointing forward where weil and denn point back. It takes first position, so the verb comes straight after — unlike denn, which sits outside its clause.

sentences.trap: deshalb inverts and denn does not, and they can translate into the same English sentence. Deshalb möchte ich Tee has möchte second because deshalb is the first element; denn ich möchte Tee has möchte second because denn is not an element at all. Two different reasons for the same-looking result.
sentences.sound: DES-halp — the h in the middle is really said, and the final b hardens to a p as a final b always does in German.

variations.display: Deshalb möchte ich Kaffee
variations.changed: a different consequence; the inversion is fixed

variations.display: Deshalb gehe ich nach Hause
variations.changed: a different verb carrying the consequence

variations.display: Deshalb arbeite ich nicht
variations.changed: a negative consequence, with nicht at the end

mistake.why: deshalb is the first element of the clause, so möchte has to be second and ich third. This is the same inversion M4 taught for fronted time words and M6 drilled ten times — the word in front is new, the law is not.

sentences.usage: The second half of an explanation, after the reason has been given.
sentences.mnemonic: deshalb takes the first seat, so the verb takes the second.

words.note: why. A question word like was, wann and wo: first position, verb after. The answer it invites can be a bare weil-clause on its own — Weil ich müde bin — verb still at the end. Normal spoken German.

sentences.trap: The answer to warum is where weil does its damage. The question is easy; the reply is the sentence where the verb has to travel, and a learner who has just heard a comfortable verb-second question will keep the same order out of momentum.
sentences.sound: va-ROOM, with the stress on the second syllable and the w said as a v. The u is the oo of "book", not the uh of English "rum".

variations.display: Warum sind Sie müde?
variations.changed: sein instead of möchten; the shape does not move

variations.display: Warum arbeiten Sie nicht?
variations.changed: a negative question, with nicht at the end and still no do anywhere

variations.display: Warum möchten Sie Kaffee?
variations.changed: a different thing asked about

mistake.why: warum is the first element, so the verb is second and Sie third: Warum möchten Sie Tee? German asks with word order alone, and there is nothing to insert in front of the subject.

sentences.usage: Asking for the reason behind what somebody has just said.
sentences.mnemonic: warum asks; weil answers, and the answer moves its verb.

words.note: thirst — a NOUN, der Durst. German states this kind of state as something you HAVE, with no article: Ich habe Durst; English says you ARE thirsty. After M5's Hunger, the second of the haben family.

sentences.trap: There is no article. Ich habe Durst, never *Ich habe den Durst or *Ich habe einen Durst — the bare noun is what makes it a state rather than a possession of some particular thirst.
sentences.sound: DOORST, one syllable, with the u as the oo of "book" and a rolled or throaty r that barely sounds before the s.

variations.display: Ich habe Hunger
variations.changed: the same construction with M5's noun in it

variations.display: Ich habe Durst, denn ich arbeite
variations.changed: a reason joined on with denn, so the verb after it stays second

variations.display: Ich habe keinen Durst
variations.changed: M3's kein negating the noun — and it takes the masculine accusative keinen

mistake.why: Durst is a noun, so this says "I am thirst". The English shape is "I am thirsty" with an adjective, and German has no adjective here at all — the state is a thing you have.

sentences.usage: Said before asking for a drink.
sentences.mnemonic: German has hunger and thirst; English is hungry and thirsty.

words.note: fear — die Angst, the third of the haben family after Hunger and Durst. English borrowed it for a modern dread; in German it is the everyday word for being afraid of anything. Bare after habe.

sentences.trap: The English borrowing narrows the word and the German original does not. Ich habe Angst is what a child says about the dark, not a diagnosis — reading the German through the English loan makes the sentence sound far more dramatic than it is.
sentences.sound: ANGST, one syllable, and the ng is the ng of "singer" with no hard g after it. The a is short and open.

variations.display: Ich habe keine Angst
variations.changed: M3's kein on a feminine noun, so keine

variations.display: Ich habe Angst, denn ich bin krank
variations.changed: a reason attached with denn, and its verb still second

variations.display: Warum haben Sie Angst?
variations.changed: the same state asked about, in the Sie form

mistake.why: Angst is a noun, so this says "I am fear". The construction is haben plus the bare noun, exactly as it is for Hunger and Durst.

sentences.usage: Admitting to a worry, in ordinary rather than clinical words.
sentences.mnemonic: Hunger, Durst, Angst — three things you have, not three things you are.

words.note: to me — the dative of ich, for something that happens to a person rather than being done by them. Two seats, one shape: M2's Mir geht es gut and this module's Mir ist kalt. The person is no subject.
cold. After ist no ending, like teuer. The sentence around it is what is not free: with a person it goes with mir; only a thing takes a plain subject — Der Kaffee ist kalt.
warm — spelled as in English, said with a swallowed r. It behaves like kalt: Mir ist warm for the person, Der Kaffee ist warm for the thing. Learn the pair together; the construction is the lesson.

sentences.trap: This sentence has no subject. There is nothing standing where English's "I" stands — mir is a dative and ist has no subject to agree with — which is why the shape feels like a sentence with a hole in it until it is learned as one piece.
sentences.sound: meer ist KALT. mir has the long ee of ie; kalt has a short open a and a clear l, said with the tongue forward rather than the dark English l.

variations.display: Mir ist warm
variations.changed: the other temperature, in the identical frame

variations.display: Ist Ihnen kalt?
variations.changed: the same construction asked of somebody else — M2's Ihnen where mir was, and the verb first

variations.display: Der Kaffee ist kalt
variations.changed: a THING is cold, so it takes an ordinary subject and no dative at all

mistake.why: This is a grammatical German sentence and it means the speaker is cold-hearted. That is why it is worth a warning rather than a footnote: the listener does not hear a foreigner's slip, they hear a claim about your character. Temperature felt by a person is Mir ist kalt.

sentences.usage: Said in a draughty room, and understood immediately.
sentences.mnemonic: The cold happens TO me, so the sentence starts with mir.

sentences.display: Ich denke, dass das Buch gut ist
sentences.cue: I think the book is good
sentences.literal: I think, that the book good is

words.note: to think — denke for ich, denken for Sie and the infinitive. It introduces an opinion; what follows is a dass-clause with its verb at the end. Ich denke alone is a complete answer, like “I think so”.
that — the conjunction, never optional: English drops it (“I think it is good”), German keeps it. It holds the second clause on and sends its verb to the end. Two s: dass this word; das the article.

sentences.trap: dass das is not a stutter and not a typo. The first word is the conjunction with two s and the second is the article with one, and they sit next to each other because German needs both: dass opens the clause, das belongs to Buch. Hearing them as one word is what makes this the sentence to hang the spelling on.
sentences.sound: Both words are said the same: DAS, with a short a and a hissed s. The ear cannot separate them at all, which is precisely why the eye has to.

variations.display: Ich denke, dass der Kaffee gut ist
variations.cue: I think the coffee is good
variations.changed: a masculine subject inside the clause; the verb is still last

variations.display: Ich denke, dass das Buch zu teuer ist
variations.cue: I think the book is too expensive
variations.changed: M8's zu teuer inside the clause, with ist still at the end behind it

variations.display: Ich denke, dass Sie müde sind
variations.changed: the Sie form inside the clause, so sind travels to the end

mistake.display: Ich denke, das Buch ist gut
mistake.why: German cannot drop the conjunction: Ich denke, dass das Buch gut ist. Leaving dass out also leaves the verb in second position, so one English habit produces two mistakes at once.

sentences.usage: Offering an opinion without insisting on it.
sentences.mnemonic: Two s opens the clause; one s belongs to the noun.

sentences.display: Ich bin traurig, weil ich krank bin
sentences.literal: I am sad, because I ill am

words.note: sad. An adjective after sein, so no ending, like müde and kalt. The final -ig is the soft ch of ich: TROW-rich, not a hard g — the same ending as billig and dreißig.
ill, sick. Another plain adjective after sein. English has borrowed it in "crank" and in medical words, but in German it is the everyday word for being unwell, from a cold to something serious.

sentences.trap: Both halves of this sentence use sein, and only one of them puts it last. The main clause has bin second and the weil-clause has bin last, in the space of eight words — which makes it the cleanest place in the module to see the rule doing its work.
sentences.sound: TROW-rich: the au is the ow of "how" and the -ig ends in the soft ch. krank has the same short open a as kalt.

variations.display: Ich bin müde, weil ich krank bin
variations.changed: a different feeling in front of the same reason

variations.display: Ich bin traurig, denn ich bin krank
variations.changed: denn instead of weil, so the verb comes back to second position

variations.display: Ich arbeite nicht, weil ich krank bin
variations.cue: I'm not working because I'm ill
variations.changed: a different main clause, with the same reason behind it

mistake.display: Ich bin traurig, weil ich bin krank
mistake.why: weil sends the finite verb to the end of its own clause: weil ich krank bin. The main clause in front of it is untouched — only the clause the conjunction opens is rearranged.

sentences.usage: Explaining why you are not yourself today.
sentences.mnemonic: One sentence, one verb second and one verb last. That is the whole module.

sentences.display: Ich bin glücklich, denn der Kaffee ist gut
sentences.cue: I'm happy, because the coffee is good

words.note: happy — from das Glück, “luck” and “happiness” at once, with the -lich ending German uses the way English uses “-ly” or “-ful”. Pursed-lip ü, soft ch, and no ending after ist.

sentences.trap: The clause after denn has a full subject of its own — der Kaffee — and its verb is still second, behind that subject. denn does not count as part of the clause it introduces, so nothing about the clause changes; that is the whole difference from weil, and a longer subject makes it easier to see.
sentences.sound: GLÜK-lich, two syllables, with the ü of pursed lips and a soft ch at the end. The -lich ending never has a hard k sound in it.

mistake.why: denn leaves the clause after it exactly as it would have stood alone: der Kaffee ist gut. Sending ist to the end applies weil's rule to a word that does not have it.

sentences.usage: Saying why something has gone right.
sentences.mnemonic: denn joins two whole sentences; weil rebuilds the second one.
